text: (a) Τὸ ἡμέτερον ἑκουσίως προσχωρήσωμεν. Active accepit Turrianus, cum ita reddit, Eam quæ nostra est, sponte ad Deum accommodemus. Ubi is, qui Baronianæ editioni præfuit, sive is ipse, non bene margini apposuit, Fort. quod nostrum est, τὸ ἡμέτερον enim, θέλημα, refert : ac bene Turrianus expressit : eam, quæ nostra est, id est, voluntas : nec hic scrupulus est, sed quod ex vet. leg. τὸ προσχωρήσωμεν activum fecit, quod nunquam aliter quam neutrum usurpari videtur. Locus quem affert vet. lex, incerto auctore, huic nostro geminus est. Προσκεχωρήκασιν τὴν γλῶσσαν πρὸς τὸ Καρικὸν ἔθνος : Accommodaverunt, aptaverunt linguam, etc. At melius Steph. γλῶσσαν accipit, pro, κατὰ γλῶσσαν, ecclipsi Græcis consuetissima, et sic erit idem ac λόγῳ, sermone, lingua, accesserunt. Hic vero Nostra voluntate sponte accedamus ; nos Deo, quasi dedititii, sponte submittamus.
anchorLine: ρον ἐκουσίως προσχωρήσωμεν (a) τῷ Θεῷ, ἐκ τοῦ
en: Our own will freely go over to (accede to) God. Turrianus took this actively, translating 'Let us accommodate that which is ours, of its own accord, to God.' Whoever supervised the Baronian edition (or Baronius himself) wrongly put in the margin 'Perhaps: that which is ours', since τὸ ἡμέτερον refers to θέλημα (will); and Turrianus rendered it well: 'that which is ours', that is, the will. Nor is there a difficulty here, except that, following an old reading, he made προσχωρήσωμεν active, which never seems to be used other than as a neuter. The passage that the old lexicon cites, from an unnamed author, is a twin of this one: 'They have attached their tongue to the Carian people', that is, 'They have accommodated, fitted, their tongue', and so on. But Stephanus better takes γλῶσσαν as standing for 'according to tongue', an ellipsis very common in Greek, and so it will be the same as 'by speech, by language, they have come over'. Here, however, it is 'Let us come over by our own will, of our own accord'; let us submit ourselves to God of our own accord, like those who have surrendered.

text: (b) Κατὰ τοῦτο ἐκλείψει. Non extant eo psalmo hæc Basilii verba, nisi Maximus ejus habuit pleniorem ἔκδοσιν, vel ex memoria citavit, sibique Basilii textum conflavit ex iis, quæ illo psal. et quæ Isa. VII, in ejus expositione legerat. Ad hunc sensum igitur exponit Basil. p. 259, non Isaiæ locum, sed ejus psalmi versum, Dilexisti justitiam, et odisti iniquitatem, quod reliqui homines labore et exercitatione, prona ad bonum malumque voluntate, ægre tandem impleant : Σοὶ δὲ φυσική τίς ἐστι πρὸς τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἡ οἰκείωσις, καὶ πρὸς τὴν ἀνομίαν ἀλλοίωσις. Tibi ad bonum naturalis necessitudo, et ab improbitate aversio, οἰκείωσις, naturalis proprietas, quod reddit interp. rudius est. Fusius dicto cap. 7, p. 1007, ubi nostris sic ad utrumque pronis, opponit. Ἀλλ' οὐχὶ καὶ ὁ Κύριος οὕτως, ἀλλ' ἡ πρὸς τὸ ἀγαθὸν αὐτοῦ οἰκείωσις, εὐθὺς ἐκ πρώτης γενέσεως διεφαίνετο. Τί γὰρ γέγραπται; « Ὅτι πρὶν ἢ γνῶναι αὐτὸν ἢ προελέσθαι πονηρὰ, ἐκλέξεται ἀγαθόν. At non sic etiam Dominus, sed ejus ad bonum necessitudo, a primo statim ortu elucescebat. Quid enim scriptum est? Antequam sciat ipse, aut præeligat mala, eliget bona. Ubi turbate interpr. Titelm. et laciniose, Sed quod erat bonum sibi vindicabat, familiariter etiam initio statim et a primordio suæ nativitatis in ipso inclaruit ; quibus nec fidem interpr. nec bonæ lucem paraph. affert. Quare illud, τὸ γὰρ πρὶν ἢ, δηλοῖ, non Basilii expositio est, ut Turr. existimavit, sive qui Baronianæ editioni præfuit, sed Maximi, Basilii verba et Isaiæ, magis explicantis.
anchorLine: δ:δάσκων, ἔφη· « Κατὰ τοῦτο δὲ ἐκλήψῃ (b) καὶ τὸ
en: 'According to this he will fail.' These words of Basil are not extant in that psalm, unless Maximus had a fuller edition of it, or cited from memory and put together for himself a text of Basil from what he had read in Basil's exposition of that psalm and of Isaiah 7. In this sense, then, Basil (p. 259) expounds not the passage of Isaiah but the verse of that psalm, 'Thou hast loved justice and hated iniquity', which other men, with a will inclined to good and evil by labour and exercise, fulfil only with difficulty: 'To thee there is a natural affinity (oikeiosis) to the good and an alteration away from iniquity.' The rendering 'natural necessity for the good, and aversion from wickedness, oikeiosis, natural property' by the interpreter is cruder. He argues more fully in the cited chapter 7, p. 1007, where he sets this against our people being thus inclined to both. 'But not so the Lord, but his affinity to the good shone forth immediately from his first coming into being. For what is written? Before he knows, or chooses evil, he will choose good.' Where the interpreter Titelman, in a confused and rambling way, has 'But what was good he claimed for himself, and familiarly even from the very beginning and from the first origin of his birth it shone forth in him'; which neither lends credit to the interpreter nor light to the paraphrast. Therefore the phrase 'for before' (to gar prin e) makes clear that this is not Basil's exposition, as Turrianus thought, or whoever supervised the Baronian edition, but Maximus's, explaining the words of Basil and of Isaiah.

text: (h) Ὅτι ὑπηγορεύθη. Accepisse videtur Maximus pro eo quod est in dicta epist. relata in vi synodo, act. 12. Τὸν προσφωνηθέντα λόγον Βιγιλίῳ ἐνταῦθα παρόντι. Sermonem acclamatorium Vigilio hic præsenti; id est, illi nuncupatum, quod et reddidi; exponitque idem Sergius in fine epistolæ, ubi narrat injunxisse Heraclium, cum Edessæ versaretur, ut excerptas ex illo libello Patrum auctoritates, de una Christi operatione unaque voluntate ad se mitteret. Τὰς ἐμφερομένας τῷ γενομένῳ, ὡς εἴρηται, παρὰ τοῦ ἐν ἁγίοις Μηνᾶ, πρὸς τὸν ἁγιώτατον Βιγίλιον δογματικῷ, περὶ μιᾶς ἐνεργείας καὶ ἑνὸς θελήματος, λόγῳ: ut paterna illi testimonia defloremus, quæ continentur in libro dogmatico (sicut dictum est) facto a sanctæ memoriæ Mena ad sanctissimum Vigilium, de una operatione et una voluntate. Acclamatorius ergo sermo Vigilio, et ad Vigilium factus, idem Sergio, ἐπαγορευθείς Maximo: illi nuncupatus; quodque Maximus negat haberi in ea epistola fuisse porrectum, ἐπιδοθέντα: eamque tamen vocem illa habeat, priore loco Epistolæ, προσφωνηθέντα καὶ ἐπιδοθέντα παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ ἐνταῦθα παρόντι Βιγιλίῳ· Dirigentes etiam sermonem acclamatorium Menæ sanctissimi quondam patriarchæ hujus a Deo conservandæ Urbis, porrectum ab eo hic præsenti Vigilio sanctæ memoriæ; alterum dicamus necesse est, vel memoria lapsum Maximum, vel corruptam Sergii epistolam. Ac primum in re sic gravi ac præsenti negotio ascribere viro accurato, durius est, præsertim acquiescente ei adversario, etsi fatetur et ipse memoriam non tenere. Subdititiam vero illam vocem in Sergii epistola indicio esse potest, quod repetendo in fine, ejus non meminit, sed unam vocem habet priori illi respondentem, uti dictum est, γενομένῳ. Alter ergo editum et nuncupatum; alter etiam porrectum, solemnique conventu coram principe ac senatu lectum ac publicatum seu præsentatum dicit: quæ pugnantia Maximus arguit; tanquam scilicet non tacituro Sergio; si hæc quoque facta essent, ut receptum a Vigilio libellum, eique probatum, ostenderet: quod Pyrrhus salagebat, suo hoc plagio, a Maximo detecto: sive alias verus Menæ liber est, sive a Monothelitis confictus, eique suppositus. Turr. quod τὸ ὑπηγορεύθη reddit commonefactum de illo libello, longe est a fide boni interpretis.
anchorLine: Ὑπηγορεύθη (h) μὲν, οὐκ ἐπεδόθη δὲ
en: On 'Ὅτι ὑπηγορεύθη': Maximus seems to have taken it for what is in the said letter, reported in the sixth synod, act 12: 'Τὸν προσφωνηθέντα λόγον Βιγιλίῳ ἐνταῦθα παρόντι.' 'The acclamatory discourse to Vigilius here present'; that is, 'dedicated to him', which I too have rendered; and Sergius himself explains it at the end of the letter, where he relates that Heraclius, when he was staying at Edessa, had enjoined that the authorities of the Fathers excerpted from that libellus, on one operation of Christ and one will, be sent to him: 'Τὰς ἐμφερομένας τῷ γενομένῳ, ὡς εἴρηται, παρὰ τοῦ ἐν ἁγίοις Μηνᾶ, πρὸς τὸν ἁγιώτατον Βιγίλιον δογματικῷ, περὶ μιᾶς ἐνεργείας καὶ ἑνὸς θελήματος, λόγῳ': that we might cull for him the paternal testimonies which are contained in the dogmatic book (as has been said) made by Menas of holy memory to the most holy Vigilius, on one operation and one will. So the acclamatory discourse, made for Vigilius and to Vigilius, is in Sergius the same as the 'ἐπαγορευθείς' of Maximus: 'dedicated to him'; and as to Maximus's denying that it is stated in that letter to have been presented, 'ἐπιδοθέντα', although the letter has that very word in its earlier place: 'προσφωνηθέντα καὶ ἐπιδοθέντα παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ ἐνταῦθα παρόντι Βιγιλίῳ' (Directing also the acclamatory discourse of Menas, of most holy memory, once patriarch of this God-preserved City, presented by him here to Vigilius of holy memory), one of two things we must say: either that Maximus slipped in memory, or that Sergius's letter is corrupted. And first, in a matter so grave and present, to ascribe it to an accurate man is harsher, especially as his adversary acquiesces, although he too confesses he does not retain it in memory. That that word is spurious in Sergius's letter can be an indication that, in repeating it at the end, he makes no mention of it, but has one word answering to that earlier one, as was said, 'γενομένῳ'. The one, then, says published and dedicated; the other says also presented, read and made public, or presented, in solemn assembly before prince and senate; discrepancies which Maximus argues, namely as though Sergius would not have kept silent, if these things too had been done, so as to show that the libellus was received by Vigilius and approved by him: which Pyrrhus was striving after, with this plagiarism of his detected by Maximus; whether otherwise the book of Menas is genuine, or was forged by the Monothelites and attributed to him. Turrianus, in that he renders 'τὸ ὑπηγορεύθη' as 'commonefactum de illo libello', is far from the good faith of an honest interpreter.

text: (j) Καὶ ὃν φησι λίβελλον. Illis scite Maximus in Sergium refundit libellum Menæ dictum, tanquam is non vere Menæ esset, sed illi suppositum a Sergio, ut tum viri auctoritate, tum falsa Vigilii susceptione Monothelismum abs se disseminatum fulciret. Unde non mirum sibi in eo Sergium Pyrrhumque dissentire, cum falsum, nec sibi, nec vero consentiat. Sic in vi synodo aperte νοθείας redarguitur ille libellus, cui in omnibus Maximus præivit, etsi ejus Honorii defensionem non est amplexa; quod ejus proscriptione visum mollire Orientalium animos, quod Martinus e concilio Lateranensi, tot capitum proscriptione ex nomine, ac quibuscum suspicio esset convenisse Honorium, gravius offendisset: in quam dispensationem ipsa Romana Ecclesia consenserit, ut satis aperte indicat Adrian. in viii synodo relatus, dum agnoscit Orientales dixisse anathema Honorio, sed de consensu nostræ sedis, Romanæ, cui præsidebat. Tanta hæc Sergii machinamenta Maximo exposita, ac Sergio successori in faciem objecta, veræ sint Monothelismi origines, non quam Theophanes collationem refert Heraclii cum Athanasio Jacobitarum patriarcha, cui et Antiochenum patriarchatum pollicitus sit, si modo is synodum reciperet, et in unitionem consentiret, cujus altum silentium, præterquam illis, qui simili chronographia, verbatim pene ipsum exscripserunt. Facitque quod Heraclius ad Joann. papam in Sergium et Constantinopolitanos, omnem ejus novitatis, et editæ ejus nomine Ecthesis, refert invidiam, cujus verba refert Maximus in Coll. cum principibus in secreto. Putemque incidisse Theophanem in alicujus Constantinopolitani minus probatam narrationem, quovis tandem animo hæc ille scripsisset, sive levandi causa suos Constantinopolitanos Sergiumque, sive præsidium quærendi Monothelismo, cui vir tantus, eaque zeli et unitionis Ecclesiarum specie, recepto cunctis consilio, exordium fecisset. Quamobrem etiam maluit Sergius Heraclianam Ecthesim dicere, quam suam, ejus professionis chartam, quam curasset ejus subscriptione muniri, ut ipse Heraclius auctor est. Sic sæpe chronologi, non magno judicio, hincinde aliis aliisque dicta, sæpe etiam alia aliis pugnantia congerunt; quæ omnia qui velit tueri, næ is laborem improbum casumque susceperit: potuitque mitius habere charissimus sodalis et commilito, P. Jacobus Goarius ὁ μακαρίτης in suo Theophane, quod pene tyro, non alio spiritu in eam rem, in meo de Monothelitarum hæresi syntagmate, scripseram.
anchorLine: ψας καὶ ὃν φησι λίβελλον (j) Μηνᾶ διὰ τῆς μεσι-
en: On 'Καὶ ὃν φησι λίβελλον': With these words Maximus neatly throws back upon Sergius the libellus called Menas's, as though it were not truly Menas's but put under his name by Sergius, in order to prop up the Monothelitism disseminated by him, both by the authority of the man and by the false reception of it by Vigilius. Whence it is no wonder that Sergius and Pyrrhus disagree with each other in it, since what is false agrees neither with itself nor with the truth. Thus in the sixth synod that libellus is openly convicted of spuriousness (νοθείας), in all of which Maximus went before, even though [the synod] did not embrace the defence of that Honorius; because it seemed that his proscription would soften the minds of the Easterners, whereas Martin, from the Lateran council, by the proscription by name of so many chapters, and of those with whom there was suspicion that Honorius had agreed, would have given graver offence: to which dispensation the Roman Church itself consented, as Adrian, cited in the eighth synod, indicates quite openly, when he acknowledges that the Easterners said anathema to Honorius, but with the consent of our see, the Roman, over which he presided. Let these so great machinations of Sergius, set out to Maximus and thrown in the face of Sergius's successor, be the true origins of Monothelitism, not the conference which Theophanes relates of Heraclius with Athanasius, patriarch of the Jacobites, to whom he had even promised the Antiochene patriarchate, if only he would receive the synod and consent to the union; of which [conference] the deep silence [is noted], except by those who in a similar chronography copied him almost word for word. And it bears on this that Heraclius, to Pope John, refers all the odium of this novelty, and of the Ecthesis published in his name, to Sergius and the Constantinopolitans; whose words Maximus reports in the Colloquy with the princes in secret. And I suppose that Theophanes fell upon the less approved narrative of some Constantinopolitan, with whatever intention he had written this, whether for the sake of relieving his Constantinopolitans and Sergius, or of seeking support for Monothelitism, to which so great a man, and with that appearance of zeal and of union of the Churches, the plan having been accepted by all, had given a beginning. Wherefore Sergius too preferred to call it the Heraclian Ecthesis rather than his own, the paper of his profession, which he had taken care to have fortified by his subscription, as Heraclius himself is the authority. So chronologists often, with no great judgment, pile together things said here and there by this one and that, often also things at odds with one another; whoever wishes to defend all of which, he will indeed undertake a wicked labour and risk: and my dearest companion and comrade, Fr. Jacques Goar, ὁ μακαρίτης, in his Theophanes could have treated more mildly what I, almost a beginner, with no different spirit in this matter, had written in my [treatise] on the heresy of the Monothelites.
